a-gift-to-young-housewives.name: A Gift to Young Housewives
a-gift-to-young-housewives.summary: A Russian cookbook by Elena Molokhovets, continually revised between 1861 and 1917, that was the most successful and widely used cookery book in Russian households of its era.

kvass.name: Kvass
kvass.summary: A fermented, low-alcoholic cereal-based drink with a sweet-and-sour taste, originating in northeastern Europe and first recorded in the Primary Chronicle's account of Vladimir the Great's baptism in 988.

chyhyryn.name: Chyhyryn
chyhyryn.summary: A city in central Ukraine that served as the capital of the Cossack Hetmanate from 1648 to 1669.

kiev-governorate.name: Kiev Governorate
kiev-governorate.summary: An administrative province of the Russian Empire and later Soviet Ukraine from 1796 to 1925, covering right-bank Ukraine with its capital at Kiev.

chernigov-governorate.name: Chernihiv Governorate
chernigov-governorate.summary: An administrative province of the Russian Empire, created in 1802 with its capital at Chernihiv; it later became a governorate of Ukrainian successor states after 1918.

poltava-governorate.name: Poltava Governorate
poltava-governorate.summary: An administrative unit of the Russian Empire created in 1802, centered on the city of Poltava and covering territory now part of central Ukraine.

yekaterina-avdeyeva.name: Yekaterina Avdeyeva
yekaterina-avdeyeva.summary: A Russian writer (1788-1865) known for books on homemaking and collections of Russian folk tales, and sister of writers Nikolai and Ksenofont Polevoy.

wincenta-zawadzka.name: Wincenta Zawadzka
wincenta-zawadzka.summary: Polish author (c. 1824–1894) of the popular cookbook Kucharka litewska (The Lithuanian Cook), first published in Vilnius in 1843 under a pen name.

zhytomyr.name: Zhytomyr
zhytomyr.summary: A city in western Ukraine's Zhytomyr Oblast, with a 2022 population of 261,624, a major transport hub and center of the country's Polish minority.

auguste-escoffier.name: Auguste Escoffier
auguste-escoffier.summary: French chef (1846–1935) who modernised French cooking, codified the five mother sauces, and created the kitchen brigade system still used today.

le-guide-culinaire.name: Le Guide Culinaire
le-guide-culinaire.summary: Georges Auguste Escoffier's 1903 cookbook of French restaurant cuisine, developed while he worked at the Savoy, Ritz and Carlton hotels; still in print.

pelmeni.name: Pelmeni
pelmeni.summary: Dumplings of filled dough considered Russia's national dish, with roots among the Komi and Udmurt; the name pelnan, meaning 'ear bread,' came from Finno-Ugric peoples introduced to the dish by Iranian merchants.

zaporozhian-cossacks.name: Zaporozhian Cossacks
zaporozhian-cossacks.summary: Cossacks living downstream of the Dnieper Rapids, mostly Ruthenian, who for centuries were a major political and military force challenging Poland-Lithuania, Russia, and the Crimean Khanate.

don-cossacks.name: Don Cossacks
don-cossacks.summary: Cossacks settled along the Don River who formed an autonomous polity in southern Russia from the late 16th century until 1918, playing a major military role in the Russian Empire.

babka.name: Babka
babka.summary: A sweet braided cake made from yeast dough with fillings such as cinnamon, chocolate or fruit, originating in Jewish communities of Poland and Western Ukraine.

latke.name: Latke
latke.summary: A potato pancake in Ashkenazi Jewish cuisine, traditionally made from shredded potatoes and egg yolk fried in oil and eaten at Hanukkah.

ukha.name: Ukha
ukha.summary: A clear Russian fish soup traditionally made with root vegetables and herbs, associated with Cossack culture of the Don region; the term earlier meant thick meat broth before shifting to fish soup.

varenyky.name: varenyky
varenyky.summary: Traditional Ukrainian dumplings of unleavened dough with sweet or savoury fillings, closely related to Polish pierogi but with thinner, softer dough.

lubny.name: Lubny
lubny.summary: City in Poltava Oblast, central Ukraine, with a population of about 44,000.

adam-kirkor.name: Adam Kirkor
adam-kirkor.summary: Polish publisher, journalist and archaeologist who lived from 1818 to 1886.

vilna-governorate.name: Vilna Governorate
vilna-governorate.summary: A province of the Russian Empire from 1795 to 1918, created from former Grand Duchy of Lithuania territory after the Third Partition of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, with its capital at Vilnius.

alexander-i-of-russia.name: Alexander I of Russia
alexander-i-of-russia.summary: Emperor of Russia from 1801 to 1825, nicknamed 'the Blessed'; he ruled through the Napoleonic Wars, pursued early liberal reforms, and became King of Congress Poland in 1815.

nicholas-i-of-russia.name: Nicholas I
nicholas-i-of-russia.summary: Emperor of Russia from 1825 to 1855, remembered as a reactionary ruler known for territorial expansion, centralised administration, and repression of dissent.

empire-style.name: Empire style
empire-style.summary: Early-19th-century design movement in architecture and decorative arts, the second phase of Neoclassicism, that flourished from 1799 to 1815 under Napoleon I and spread across Europe and the US.

neo-byzantine-architecture.name: Neo-Byzantine architecture
neo-byzantine-architecture.summary: A 19th-century revival style drawing on Byzantine church architecture of Constantinople, seen in buildings such as Paris's Sacré-Coeur and across the Russian Empire.

russian-revival-architecture.name: Russian Revival style
russian-revival-architecture.summary: A 19th-century Russian architectural movement blending Byzantine and older pre-Petrine Russian elements, a skilled stylization rather than a direct copy of past architecture.

a-life-for-the-tsar.name: A Life for the Tsar
a-life-for-the-tsar.summary: An 1836 opera by Mikhail Glinka about Ivan Susanin, a 17th-century patriotic hero who died resisting a Polish invasion on behalf of the newly elected first Romanov tsar.

mikhail-glinka.name: Mikhail Glinka
mikhail-glinka.summary: Russian composer (1804–1857), the first to gain wide recognition within Russia, regarded as the fountainhead of Russian classical music and a major influence on later Russian composers.

ruslan-and-lyudmila-opera.name: Ruslan and Lyudmila
ruslan-and-lyudmila-opera.summary: An 1837–1842 opera by Mikhail Glinka based on Alexander Pushkin's narrative poem, best known today for its overture.

peredvizhniki.name: Peredvizhniki
peredvizhniki.summary: A group of Russian realist painters, also called the Wanderers, who broke from academic restrictions and formed a cooperative for travelling art exhibitions from 1870.

alexander-ii-of-russia.name: Alexander II of Russia
alexander-ii-of-russia.summary: Emperor of Russia from 1855 until his assassination in 1881, known as 'the Liberator' for his 1861 edict abolishing serfdom and for other liberal reforms early in his reign.

ivan-shishkin.name: Ivan Shishkin
ivan-shishkin.summary: Russian Realist landscape painter and draughtsman (1832–1898), a founding member of the Peredvizhniki group of artists.

ilya-repin.name: Ilya Repin
ilya-repin.summary: A Ukrainian-born Russian painter (1844–1930), one of the most renowned artists in 19th-century Russia, known for works like Barge Haulers on the Volga and portraits of figures such as Leo Tolstoy.

isaac-levitan.name: Isaac Levitan
isaac-levitan.summary: Russian landscape painter (1860–1900) who advanced the genre of the 'mood landscape.'

the-five-composers.name: The Mighty Handful
the-five-composers.summary: Five 19th-century Russian composers (Balakirev, Cui, Mussorgsky, Rimsky-Korsakov and Borodin) who worked together in Saint Petersburg from 1856 to 1870 to create a distinct national style of classical music.

russian-musical-society.name: Russian Musical Society
russian-musical-society.summary: The first music school in Russia open to the public, launched in 1859 by Grand Duchess Elena Pavlovna and pianist Anton Rubinstein; disbanded in the Russian Revolution and later revived.

pyotr-ilyich-tchaikovsky.name: Tchaikovsky
pyotr-ilyich-tchaikovsky.summary: Russian Romantic composer (1840–1893) whose works, including Swan Lake, The Nutcracker and the 1812 Overture, were the first by a Russian to gain lasting international fame.

sergei-rachmaninoff.name: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sergei-rachmaninoff.summary: Russian composer, virtuoso pianist and conductor (1873–1943), widely considered one of the last great representatives of Romanticism in Russian classical music.

ucha-river.name: Ucha River
ucha-river.summary: A 42 km river in Moscow Oblast, Russia, flowing through the towns of Pushkino and Ivanteyevka into the Klyazma.

taras-shevchenko.name: Taras Shevchenko
taras-shevchenko.summary: Ukrainian poet, writer and artist (1814–1861) whose poetry collection Kobzar is considered the foundation of modern Ukrainian literature.

vienna-secession.name: Vienna Secession
vienna-secession.summary: An 1897 Austrian art movement related to Art Nouveau, formed by artists including Gustav Klimt who broke away from a more traditional artists' association.

zhmerynka.name: Zhmerynka
zhmerynka.summary: A city in Vinnytsia Oblast, central Ukraine, with a 2022 population of about 33,754, administrative center of Zhmerynka Raion.

lviv.name: Lviv
lviv.summary: The largest city in western Ukraine, named after Leo I of Galicia; it was capital of the Kingdom of Galicia–Volhynia (1272–1340), then passed through Polish, Habsburg Austrian, and Soviet rule.

lubok.name: Lubok
lubok.summary: Simple, narrative Russian print used to decorate homes and inns from the late 17th to 19th centuries, sometimes appearing in series seen as forerunners of the comic strip.

vasyl-krychevsky.name: Vasyl Krychevsky
vasyl-krychevsky.summary: A Ukrainian painter, architect, art scholar and graphic artist (1873–1952) who designed Ukraine's 1918 coat of arms, state seals and banknotes.

ukrainian-baroque.name: Ukrainian Baroque
ukrainian-baroque.summary: An artistic style, also called Cossack Baroque, that blended local traditions with European Baroque and spread across Ukraine in the 17th and 18th centuries.

w-adys-aw-horodecki.name: Władysław Horodecki
w-adys-aw-horodecki.summary: Polish architect (1863-1930) active in the Russian Empire, best known for shaping Kyiv's urban development with buildings such as the House with Chimaeras and the National Art Museum of Ukraine.

jan-matejko.name: Jan Matejko
jan-matejko.summary: Polish painter (1838–1893), a leading history painter known for depicting key moments in Polish history and sometimes called Poland's national painter.

tereshchenko-family.name: Tereshchenko family
tereshchenko-family.summary: A Ukrainian family of businessmen, entrepreneurs and philanthropists with Cossack roots, prominent from the 18th century onward.

nicholas-ii.name: Nicholas II
nicholas-ii.summary: Last emperor of Russia, reigning from 1894 until his 1917 abdication ended the Romanov dynasty; he and his family were killed in 1918.

mykola-biliashivskyi.name: Mykola Biliashivsky
mykola-biliashivskyi.summary: A Ukrainian archaeologist, ethnographer and art historian (1867–1926), a member of the All-Ukrainian Academy of Sciences and the Shevchenko Scientific Society.

potocki-palace-lviv.name: Potocki Palace
potocki-palace-lviv.summary: A grand palace in Lviv built in the 1880s as the residence of Alfred Józef Potocki, a former Minister-President of Austria; it now houses a branch of the Lviv National Art Gallery.

napoleon.name: Napoleon
napoleon.summary: French emperor from 1804 to 1814, and briefly in 1815, who rose to power as a general during the French Revolution and led sweeping military campaigns across Europe and the Middle East.

french-invasion-of-russia.name: French invasion of Russia
french-invasion-of-russia.summary: Napoleon's 1812 invasion of Russia to enforce a blockade on Britain, one of history's most devastating campaigns, costing around a million lives in under six months.

caucasian-war.name: Caucasian War
caucasian-war.summary: A 19th-century conflict in which the Russian Empire fought peoples of the North Caucasus, such as the Adyghe, Chechens and Dagestanis, who resisted Russian conquest.

treaty-of-portsmouth.name: Treaty of Portsmouth
treaty-of-portsmouth.summary: 1905 treaty ending the Russo-Japanese War, negotiated with US President Theodore Roosevelt's help; it gave Japan dominance in Korea, the Liaodong lease and southern Sakhalin.

theodore-roosevelt.name: Theodore Roosevelt
theodore-roosevelt.summary: 26th president of the United States (1901–1909), who became president after William McKinley's assassination and, before politics, wrote a history of the Naval War of 1812.

battle-of-galicia.name: Battle of Galicia
battle-of-galicia.summary: A major 1914 World War I battle in which Russia decisively defeated Austria-Hungary, capturing Lemberg (Lviv) and holding Eastern Galicia for about nine months.

galicia-eastern-europe.name: Galicia
galicia-eastern-europe.summary: A historical region spanning southeastern Poland and western Ukraine, named after the medieval city of Halych, once part of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and later Austria's Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria.

neman.name: Neman River
neman.summary: A 937-km river rising in Belarus and flowing through Lithuania to the Baltic Sea, one of Eastern Europe's major waterways.

michael-andreas-barclay-de-tolly.name: Barclay de Tolly
michael-andreas-barclay-de-tolly.summary: A Russian field marshal (1761–1818) of Baltic German descent who served as Minister of War and commanded Russia's largest army against Napoleon's 1812 invasion.

pyotr-bagration.name: Pyotr Bagration
pyotr-bagration.summary: Russian general of Georgian princely origin (1765–1812) who fought through the Napoleonic Wars, distinguished himself at Schöngrabern and Austerlitz, and commanded troops during Napoleon's 1812 invasion of Russia.

smolensk.name: Smolensk
smolensk.summary: A Russian city on the Dnieper River, first mentioned in 863, long a contested regional capital between Lithuania, Poland and Russia, and the site of battles in 1812 and 1941.

combined-fleet.name: Combined Fleet
combined-fleet.summary: The main sea-going force of the Imperial Japanese Navy, made a permanent organization only from 1933 after earlier existing as a temporary wartime command.

battle-of-tsushima.name: Battle of Tsushima
battle-of-tsushima.summary: The final, decisive naval battle of the Russo-Japanese War in May 1905, in which Japan's fleet destroyed Russia's Baltic Fleet after its seven-month voyage, the first major clash of modern steel battleship fleets.

battle-of-austerlitz.name: Battle of Austerlitz
battle-of-austerlitz.summary: The decisive 2 December 1805 battle of the War of the Third Coalition, in which Napoleon's Grande Armée defeated a combined Russian and Austrian army led by Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II.

war-of-the-fourth-coalition.name: War of the Fourth Coalition
war-of-the-fourth-coalition.summary: An 1806–1807 war in which Napoleon's France decisively defeated Prussia and fought Russia to an inconclusive standstill, after Prussia declared war fearing growing French power.

battle-of-eylau.name: Battle of Eylau
battle-of-eylau.summary: A bloody, inconclusive battle fought on 7-8 February 1807 between Napoleon's Grande Armée and the Russian army near Preussisch Eylau in East Prussia.

imam-shamil.name: Imam Shamil
imam-shamil.summary: Third Imam of the Caucasian Imamate (1840–1859) and Naqshbandi Sufi leader who led North Caucasian resistance to Imperial Russia in the 1800s.

leo-tolstoy.name: Leo Tolstoy
leo-tolstoy.summary: A Russian writer (1828–1910) regarded as one of history's greatest novelists, author of War and Peace, Anna Karenina and Resurrection, who later underwent a spiritual crisis and became a Christian anarchist and pacifist.

mikhail-lermontov.name: Mikhail Lermontov
mikhail-lermontov.summary: Russian Romantic poet, writer and painter (1814–1841), called 'the poet of the Caucasus' and considered the greatest Russian poet after Pushkin, whose prose founded the Russian psychological novel.

valerik-river.name: Valerik
valerik-river.summary: A short river in Chechnya, about 29 kilometres long, a tributary of the Sunzha with a small drainage basin.

dominic-lieven.name: Dominic Lieven
dominic-lieven.summary: English research professor at Cambridge University, a Senior Research Fellow of Trinity College and Fellow of the British Academy, born in 1952.

vasily-zhukovsky.name: Vasily Zhukovsky
vasily-zhukovsky.summary: The foremost Russian poet of the 1810s (1783–1852), a court tutor to future tsar Alexander II, credited with introducing Romanticism to Russia through wide-ranging translations.

alexander-pushkin.name: Alexander Pushkin
alexander-pushkin.summary: A Russian poet, playwright and novelist (1799–1837) of the Romantic era, considered the founder of modern Russian literature; author of Eugene Onegin.

russian-symbolism.name: Russian symbolism
russian-symbolism.summary: A Russian literary and artistic movement of the late 19th and early 20th centuries that arose separately from West European symbolism, emphasizing mysticism and defamiliarization.

silver-age-of-russian-poetry.name: Silver Age of Russian Poetry
silver-age-of-russian-poetry.summary: A richly creative era in Russian poetry from the 1890s to the 1920s, named to echo an earlier Golden Age and marked by growing recognition of women writers.

sophiology.name: Sophiology
sophiology.summary: A school of thought in Russian Orthodox Christianity holding that Divine Wisdom, or Sophia, is identified with God's essence and expressed as wisdom in the created world.

defamiliarization.name: Defamiliarization
defamiliarization.summary: An artistic technique, named by Russian formalist critics, of presenting familiar things in a strange way so audiences see them afresh; it influenced movements from Dadaism to postmodernism.

valuev-circular.name: Valuev Circular
valuev-circular.summary: An 1863 decree by Russia's interior minister Pyotr Valuev that banned religious and educational publications in the Ukrainian language, except literary works.

ems-ukaz.name: Ems Ukaz
ems-ukaz.summary: An 1876 decree by Emperor Alexander II of Russia banning the printing and import of Ukrainian-language publications, plays, and lectures, sharply limiting the language's development in the Russian Empire.

shevchenko-scientific-society.name: Shevchenko Scientific Society
shevchenko-scientific-society.summary: A Ukrainian scholarly society founded in 1873, banned under Soviet rule after 1940 and revived in 1989, named after poet Taras Shevchenko.

prosvita.name: Prosvita
prosvita.summary: An enlightenment society founded in 19th-century Austria-Hungary's Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria to preserve Ukrainian culture, education and science, as a counterbalance to Russophile trends.

kobzar-poetry-collection.name: Kobzar
kobzar-poetry-collection.summary: A book of poems by Ukrainian poet Taras Shevchenko, first published in 1840, whose title became Shevchenko's nickname and a symbol of Ukrainian national and literary revival.

antoni-malczewski.name: Antoni Malczewski
antoni-malczewski.summary: Polish Romantic poet (1793–1826) remembered for his only work, the pessimistic narrative poem Maria (1825).

j-zef-bohdan-zaleski.name: Józef Bohdan Zaleski
j-zef-bohdan-zaleski.summary: Polish Romantic poet (1802–1886), a friend of Adam Mickiewicz, who founded the Ukrainian poetic school.

tymko-padura.name: Tymko Padura
tymko-padura.summary: Romantic poet, musician and composer (1801–1871) of the Ukrainian school; his ballad about Ustym Karmaliuk became a popular Ukrainian folk song, and he took part in the November Uprising.

aleksander-groza.name: Aleksander Groza
aleksander-groza.summary: Polish poet and writer (1807–1875), part of the Ukrainian school of Polish Romantic poets and co-organizer of the almanac "Rusałka."

mykhailo-hrushevsky.name: Mykhailo Hrushevsky
mykhailo-hrushevsky.summary: A Ukrainian historian, academician and statesman (1866–1934), regarded as the country's greatest modern historian and a leading figure of the Ukrainian national revival, who later headed Ukraine's 1917–18 revolutionary parliament.

dnieper-ukraine.name: Dnieper Ukraine
dnieper-ukraine.summary: A historical term for territory along the middle Dnieper river, seen as the heartland of Ukraine, used especially for Russian-controlled Ukraine after the partitions of Poland.

polish-lithuanian-commonwealth.name: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
polish-lithuanian-commonwealth.summary: A federative union of the Kingdom of Poland and Grand Duchy of Lithuania from 1569 to 1795, one of Europe's largest and most populous states, known for its elective monarchy called the Golden Liberty.

johann-wolfgang-von-goethe.name: Goethe
johann-wolfgang-von-goethe.summary: German polymath (1749–1832) widely regarded as the most influential writer in the German language, who also wrote scientific treatises on botany, anatomy and colour and served on the Duke of Weimar's privy council.

friedrich-schiller.name: Friedrich Schiller
friedrich-schiller.summary: A German playwright, poet and historian considered one of Germany's most important classical writers, who developed Weimar Classicism with Goethe.

ivan-franko.name: Ivan Franko
ivan-franko.summary: Ukrainian poet, writer and political activist (1856–1916) who founded Western Ukraine's socialist-nationalist movement and translated many major European writers into Ukrainian.

alexander-pypin.name: Alexander Pypin
alexander-pypin.summary: A 19th-century Russian literary historian and ethnographer (1833–1904), known for his multi-volume histories of Slavic and Russian literature.

rus-people.name: Rus'
rus-people.summary: An early medieval people, generally held to be Norsemen mainly from Sweden, who settled and ruled trade routes between the Baltic and Black Sea from the 8th to 11th centuries and gave their name to Russia.

bohdan-lepky.name: Bohdan Lepky
bohdan-lepky.summary: Ukrainian writer, poet, scholar and artist (1872–1941), son of a Ukrainian writer and Greek Catholic priest.

jagiellonian-university.name: Jagiellonian University
jagiellonian-university.summary: Public university in Kraków founded in 1364 by King Casimir III the Great, the oldest university in Poland and among the oldest continuously operating in the world.

ivan-kotliarevsky.name: Ivan Kotliarevsky
ivan-kotliarevsky.summary: Ukrainian writer and poet (1769–1838) regarded as the pioneer of modern Ukrainian literature, best known for his poem Eneida, a travesty of Virgil's Aeneid.

aleksey-pisemsky.name: Aleksey Pisemsky
aleksey-pisemsky.summary: Russian novelist and dramatist (1821–1881), regarded as an equal of Turgenev and Dostoyevsky in the 1850s for his realistic depictions of Russian life.

nikolai-leskov.name: Nikolai Leskov
nikolai-leskov.summary: Russian novelist and short-story writer (1831–1895) praised for his distinctive style, whose works include "Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk" and "The Enchanted Wanderer."

viktor-klyushnikov.name: Viktor Klyushnikov
viktor-klyushnikov.summary: Russian writer and journalist (1841–1892) whose 1864 debut novel Marevo was hailed as one of the era's leading anti-nihilist novels, though his later work never matched its success.

alexander-mozhaysky.name: Alexander Mozhaysky
alexander-mozhaysky.summary: An admiral in the Imperial Russian Navy (1825–1890) and a pioneer of heavier-than-air aircraft design.

konstantin-tsiolkovsky.name: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky
konstantin-tsiolkovsky.summary: Russian scientist (1857–1935) considered a founding father of modern rocketry and astronautics, whose work later inspired Wernher von Braun and Soviet rocket engineers; lived as a recluse near Kaluga, southwest of Moscow.

lie-metchnikoff.name: Ilya Mechnikov
lie-metchnikoff.summary: Zoologist from the Russian Empire who discovered phagocytosis, a key immune process, in 1882; shared the 1908 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Paul Ehrlich.

podil.name: Podil
podil.summary: A historic neighborhood in Kyiv on the Dnieper floodplain, long the birthplace of the city's trade, commerce and administration.

yaremche.name: Yaremche
yaremche.summary: Town in western Ukraine's Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast, set in the Carpathians at about 580 metres elevation, with a 2022 population of roughly 7,900.

vladimir-chikolev.name: Vladimir Chikolev
vladimir-chikolev.summary: Russian electrical engineer (1845–1898) who founded the company Elektrotekhnik.

lviv-polytechnic.name: Lviv Polytechnic
lviv-polytechnic.summary: A public technical university in Lviv, Ukraine, founded in 1816; it is now the country's largest institution of higher education and top-ranked technical university.

kharkiv-polytechnic-institute.name: Kharkiv Polytechnic Institute
kharkiv-polytechnic-institute.summary: A public technical university founded in 1885 in Kharkiv, Ukraine, the second-oldest technical university in both the former Russian Empire and modern Ukraine.

nikolai-kibalchich.name: Nikolai Kibalchich
nikolai-kibalchich.summary: Russian revolutionary and rocket pioneer (1853–1881) who was the main explosives expert in the assassination of Tsar Alexander II.

project-orion-nuclear-propulsion.name: Project Orion
project-orion-nuclear-propulsion.summary: A 1950s and 1960s US study into a spacecraft propelled by a series of atomic explosions, abandoned partly because of the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty.

pale-of-settlement.name: Pale of Settlement
pale-of-settlement.summary: A western region of the Russian Empire, existing from 1791 to 1917, where Jewish residents were mostly required to live, established under Catherine the Great after Russia's partition of Poland.

holy-alliance.name: Holy Alliance
holy-alliance.summary: A coalition of Austria, Prussia and Russia formed after Napoleon's defeat in 1815, aimed at restraining liberalism and secularism in Europe.

pogrom.name: Pogrom
pogrom.summary: A violent riot aimed at massacring or expelling an ethnic or religious group; the term entered English to describe attacks on Jews in the late 19th-century Russian Empire.

kiev-pogrom-1881.name: Kiev pogrom (1881)
kiev-pogrom-1881.summary: A three-day wave of anti-Jewish violence in Kiev starting 26 April 1881, considered the worst of the pogroms sweeping southwestern Imperial Russia that year, triggered by the assassination of Tsar Alexander II.

datsan-gunzechoinei.name: Datsan Gunzechoinei
datsan-gunzechoinei.summary: A large Buryat Buddhist temple built in Saint Petersburg, Russia, in the early 20th century, the northernmost Buddhist temple in Europe.

russian-cosmism.name: Russian cosmism
russian-cosmism.summary: A late 19th- and early 20th-century Russian movement blending science, religion and metaphysics, holding that humanity could achieve immortality and a cosmic destiny through technology.

russian-nihilist-movement.name: Russian nihilist movement
russian-nihilist-movement.summary: A late 19th-century Russian philosophical and revolutionary movement that attacked morality, religion and traditional society, giving rise to the broader philosophy of nihilism.

nikolai-fyodorov-philosopher.name: Nikolai Fyodorov
nikolai-fyodorov-philosopher.summary: Russian religious philosopher (1829–1903) who founded Russian cosmism, advocating scientific resurrection of the dead and physical immortality; influenced Tsiolkovsky and Scriabin.

peter-kropotkin.name: Peter Kropotkin
peter-kropotkin.summary: Russian anarchist political philosopher and geographer (1842–1921), a leading proponent of anarchist communism who wrote The Conquest of Bread and Mutual Aid.

panpsychism.name: Panpsychism
panpsychism.summary: A philosophical view, one of the oldest in philosophy of mind, holding that consciousness is a fundamental feature present throughout all matter and reality.

fyodor-dostoevsky.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
fyodor-dostoevsky.summary: A Russian novelist and philosopher (1821–1881) regarded as one of the greatest in world literature, best known for Crime and Punishment, The Idiot and The Brothers Karamazov.

notes-from-underground.name: Notes from Underground
notes-from-underground.summary: A 1864 novella by Fyodor Dostoevsky presented as the confession of a bitter, isolated narrator, often read as an attack on determinism.

nikolay-chernyshevsky.name: Nikolay Chernyshevsky
nikolay-chernyshevsky.summary: Russian literary and social critic, journalist and socialist philosopher (1828–1889), the dominant intellectual figure of Russia's 1860s revolutionary democratic movement despite years of exile in Siberia.

samovar.name: Samovar
samovar.summary: A metal container, originating in Russia, traditionally used to heat water for making tea, historically fueled by coal or kindling.

odesan-russian.name: Odesan Russian
odesan-russian.summary: A vernacular variety of Russian that originated in Odesa, Ukraine, shaped by strong Ukrainian and Yiddish influences along with borrowings from Polish, French, Greek and Turkish.

kyakhta-trade.name: Kyakhta trade
kyakhta-trade.summary: Trade between Russia and China through the border town of Kyakhta from 1727, mainly exchanging Siberian furs for Chinese cotton, silk, tobacco and tea.

wissotzky-tea.name: Wissotzky Tea
wissotzky-tea.summary: Family-owned tea company founded in Moscow in 1849 that became the largest tea firm in the Russian Empire and, by the early 20th century, the world's largest tea manufacturer.

alexander-ostrovsky.name: Alexander Ostrovsky
alexander-ostrovsky.summary: A 19th-century Russian playwright (1823–1886) regarded as the leading figure of Russian realist drama, author of 47 plays still widely performed.

vlas-doroshevich.name: Vlas Doroshevich
vlas-doroshevich.summary: Russian journalist, novelist, essayist and drama critic (1864–1922), one of Russia's most popular and widely read writers of his era.
